### Overview
This repository provides the **BayesFuseMR** R package to implement our Bayesian fused shrinkage model for MR studies, along with scripts to reproduce the simulations and results described in our ongoing manuscript.

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  width = 60,
  tidy = FALSE,
  collapse = FALSE
)
```

### Installation
You first need to install the latest release of the **cmdstanr** R package with
```{r cmdstanr setup, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("cmdstanr", repos = c('https://stan-dev.r-universe.dev', getOption("repos")))
```

If you don't already have CmdStan installed then, in addition to installing the R package, it is also necessary to install CmdStan using CmdStanR's `install_cmdstan()` function. A suitable C++ toolchain is also required. Instructions are provided in the [Getting started with CmdStanR](https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/articles/cmdstanr.html) vignette. You can install the **BayesFuseMR** R package from GitHub using the `devtools` package:

```{r BayesFuseMR setup, eval= FALSE}
devtools::install_github("julstpierre/BayesFuseMR")
```

We can now load the package like any other R package. We’ll also load the **bayesplot** and **dplyr** packages to use later in examples.
```{r libraries, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(BayesFuseMR)
library(bayesplot)
library(dplyr)
```

### Load example data
We provide a dummy dataset in the package to illustrate how to use the `fit_BayesFuseMR()` function. This dataset contains simulated summary statistics from 30 SNPs for one continuous exposure and one continuous outcome.
```{r load-data}
data("dummy_data")
head(dummy_data)
```

### Running MCMC
The function `fit_BayesFuseMR()` fits a Bayesian fused shrinkage model using MCMC. It takes as input the estimated effect sizes for the exposure and outcome with their standard errors, and returns a fitted `cmdstanr` object. We can use a seed when sampling for reproducibility.
```{r fit-model, message = FALSE}
fit <- fit_BayesFuseMR(
  beta_hat_y = dummy_data$beta_hat_y,
  beta_hat_x = dummy_data$beta_hat_x,
  sigma_y = dummy_data$sigma_y,
  sigma_x = dummy_data$sigma_x,
  snps = paste0("SNP", 1:nrow(dummy_data)),
  seed = 123
)
```

### Posterior summary statistics
You can use the `summary` method to get posterior summaries of all parameters. Here, we combine the SNP identifiers with the posterior summaries of the `theta` parameter, which represents the ratio estimate for each variant.
```{r summary}
fit_summary <- cbind(snp = fit$snps, fit$posterior$summary(variables = c("theta")))
head(fit_summary)
```

### Posterior draws
You can extract the posterior draws for further analysis or visualization. The `draws()` method returns a `draws_df` object, which can be converted to a data frame for easier manipulation. For example, we can look at the trace plots and density plots of the posterior draws for the `theta` parameter to ensure convergence of the MCMC chains.
```{r trace plots, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6}
# Trace plots for theta
mcmc_trace(fit$posterior$draws("theta"))
```

```{r density plots, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6}
# Density plots for theta
mcmc_dens_chains(fit$posterior$draws("theta"))
```

### Clustering
The function `clust_BayesFuseMR()` identifies clusters and computes weighted cluster means, standard errors, and confidence intervals. We can select the number of clusters using the FDR argument which controls the false discovery rate threshold for cluster selection. Here, we set it to 0.4.
```{r clust}
clust_BayesFuseMR(fit, FDR = 0.4) %>% 
  print(n=Inf)
```
